size.note: Total standing height, rather than shoulder height, is the usual published measurement. Wikipedia gives 4.3–5.7 m for males, with females shorter. Animal Diversity Web (under the older combination Giraffa camelopardalis) gives bulls 5.7 m in total height and 3.3 m at the shoulder, with a neck of 2.4 m, and says cows are 0.7–1 m shorter than bulls. Tail length is 80–100 cm on Wikipedia and 76–101 cm on Animal Diversity Web. Mass was published only as averages (1,192 kg for males and 828 kg for females on Wikipedia) or as upper bounds (bulls up to 1,930 kg and cows up to 1,180 kg on Animal Diversity Web), so massKg is omitted. Newborns are 1.7–2 m tall (Wikipedia) or 2 m at the shoulder and 50–55 kg (Animal Diversity Web). Ossicones may reach 13.5 cm. No sexed shoulder-height range was found.

summary: The tallest land mammal, with a very long neck, long legs, and a coat of dark, somewhat rounded patches on a tawny ground, running down the legs and getting smaller. Both sexes have skin-covered ossicones. Kruger holds a large, year-round population of the southern giraffe.
description: The South African form of the southern giraffe, the one in Kruger, has dark, somewhat rounded patches with some fine projections on a tawny background. The spots extend down the legs and become smaller. Bulls are taller than cows, and their ossicones are thicker, with the hair often worn smooth; cows have thinner, tufted ossicones. The median lump on the forehead is less developed in this form than in some others. A short erect mane runs along the neck, and the long tail ends in a dark tuft. Each animal's patch pattern is unique. The tongue is long, dark and prehensile.
habits: Giraffes live in loose, open groups of related females and their young, or in bachelor groups of males; older bulls often become more solitary. They are not territorial. Animals browse through savanna and woodland, and may gather on open ground where mothers can watch for predators. They can defend themselves with powerful kicks. In Kruger the species is a year-round resident.

diet.summary: A browser of leaves, flowers, fruits and shoots of woody plants, including acacias, taken at heights most other herbivores cannot reach. An adult may eat around 34 kg of plant matter a day. They also take shrubs, and sometimes grass and fruit.
items: leaves, flowers, fruits and shoots of woody plants, including acacias

young: A single calf is usual, after a gestation of about 400–460 days (about 457 days in one compilation). The cow gives birth standing, and the calf falls to the ground. A newborn is about 1.7–2 m tall and can stand and suckle within hours. Mothers with calves may gather in nursery groups, sometimes leaving calves with one female while they forage. Calves first ruminate at four to six months and are weaned by about six to eight months in one account, or 12–16 months in another. Exact calving months for Kruger were not found.
habitat: Savanna and woodland with browse trees. In Kruger it is widespread, and one source notes that it is seen less often in the mopane country of the north.

population.notes: Some sources claim a 2023 Kruger population of 10,345–14,554 giraffe, with a point estimate of 12,412. SANParks is described as reporting an increasing trend. A more accurate figure may be available at this URL: https://www.sanparks.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/KNP-wildlife-trends.pdf. An earlier Kruger estimate of 7,427–10,876 animals in 2013 is kept here as a previous estimate. Regional Red List status is Least Concern.

previousEstimates.notes: Kruger only, cited on the EWT Southern giraffe page as Ferreira and Ellis (2013) or Ferreira et al. (2013).

viewNotes.note: A very long neck and legs, high shoulders, and a sloping back. Dark rounded patches run down onto the legs.
The long legs and tufted tail are clear from behind, and the animal often looks back over its shoulder.
Young animals may show tousled hair on the ossicones and a shaggy mane.
Loose groups often include adults of different sizes and one or more shorter young animals.

calls.description: Giraffes communicate with snorts, hisses, coughs, moans, grunts, growls and flute-like sounds. Courting males may cough loudly, females bellow to their young, and calves bleat, moo or mew. Snorting and hissing are associated with vigilance.
